info.title: Orebit Auth API
info.description:
Authentication and account API for Orebit.

## Shape

Thirty paths, forty operations. Eleven of them are **single routes carrying a discriminated union body** —
`POST /auth/register` and `/auth/login` both dispatch on `step`, `/settings/security/payment-pin/verify`
on `method`, and `/auth/session`, `/auth/password`, `/auth/device`, `/auth/2fa`,
`/settings/security/payment-pin`, `/settings/security/email`, `/settings/security/password` and
`/settings/security/anti-phishing` on `action`. Each arm is modelled here as its own schema under a
`oneOf`; eight of the eleven also carry an OpenAPI `discriminator`, so tooling can resolve a body to
exactly one shape without trying each arm in turn.

## Conventions

- **Success** is always `{ "data": ... }`. Every `POST` returns **201**; the `GET` operations return **200**.
- **Errors** are RFC 9457 `application/problem+json`. Branch on the machine-readable `type` slug, never on
  `title`. Field-level failures arrive in `errors[]`; operation-specific context in `extra`.
- **No global prefix and no versioning.** Paths are literally `/auth/login`.

## Authentication

**A browser holds one cookie and no tokens.** `orebit_session` is an opaque handle naming a server-side
record that holds the access and refresh tokens; the backend rotates them itself, on whichever ordinary
request finds the access token near expiry. Nothing on the page can read either token, and no response body
contains one — so an XSS steals a value that authorises nothing off our origin.

That is the whole of the client contract:

1. Send every request with `credentials: 'include'`.
2. Echo the `orebit_csrf` cookie in the `X-Orebit-Csrf` header on every unsafe method, or the answer is
   `403 csrf_invalid`. Safe methods need no token.
3. Never send an `Authorization` header, and never look for a token to store.

Authentication is **default-on**: a global guard covers every route and public ones opt out explicitly, so a
route added without a decorator fails closed.

`Authorization: Bearer <token>` still works, and is kept for callers that are **not** browsers — a script, an
integration test, a service. Same token, same verification, no CSRF requirement (nothing is attached
ambiently, so there is nothing to forge).

A session expires after **24 hours idle**, or at the end of a trusted device's remember-me window. Activity
pushes the deadline out; nothing else does. Rotation is enforced and single-use, and replaying a spent
refresh token still revokes the entire session family — but because rotation is now the backend's own doing,
a rotation that commits and fails to publish is **repaired** rather than read as theft.

The service sets three cookies. Only `orebit_session` is a credential; the other two cannot identify an
account on their own.

**There is no temporary signup or login cookie.** An in-flight registration is named by a `signupId` and an
in-flight sign-in by a `loginId`, both opaque 32-byte handles that travel in the request body — see
`POST /auth/register` and `POST /auth/login`. They are flow credentials, not sessions: hold one in memory
for the life of the flow, never in `localStorage`, and expect it to stop working the moment the flow
completes. The `orebit_reg` cookie and its `X-Registration-Token` header alternative have both been
removed.

- `orebit_session` — the session handle. HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, `Path=/`, Max-Age seven days, Secure in
  production. It survives every rotation, so it changes only when you sign in again.
- `orebit_csrf` — the CSRF token, deliberately **not** HttpOnly because the client has to read it to echo
  it. `Path=/`, same lifetime as its partner. Signed and bound to the session handle, so a pair planted by a
  sibling subdomain does not verify and a pair from one session is useless against another. A client on
  another origin cannot read it and should take the value from `GET /auth/session` or `GET /auth/me`.
- `orebit_device` — an opaque, HttpOnly browser-profile ID scoped to `Path=/auth`, issued on first contact
  and kept for a year. It exists to group the sessions minted by one browser's tabs, which is what makes
  `action: logout` end **every tab on the calling device** while leaving the user's other devices signed in,
  and to decide whether a trusted device's remember-me window survives a rotation. Send
  `credentials: 'include'` or the browser will withhold it, and each login will be treated as a new device.

## Things worth knowing before integrating

- **Captcha is verified against the live provider on every gated request.** There is no bypass in any
  environment.
- **Several endpoints are deliberately non-diagnostic.** `login` with `step: otp-request` always answers
  `otp_sent` — for unknown, disabled and blocked accounts alike, and the flow advances identically in every
  case so the following step gives nothing away either. This is anti-enumeration, not a malfunction.
- **Email OTP is a universal sign-in method**, not only the passwordless path: any active, unblocked account
  can receive a login code. It is what replaced forgot-password, so whoever controls the mailbox controls the
  account.
- **`503 session_store_unavailable` means retry, not sign in again.** The store in front of the session was
  unreachable; the session is probably fine, and the cookies are deliberately left in place.

## Four changes that break older clients

- **`POST /auth/login` discriminates on `step`, not `mode`, and begins with `step: start`.** A client that
  posts `{mode: 'password', ...}` gets `400 validation_failed`. Keep the
  `loginId` it returns, and send it on every later step including `POST /auth/2fa/verify` — where it
  replaces `loginId`. `otp-verify` no longer accepts an `identifier`. Registration is unchanged in shape
  but now needs `signupId` in the body on every step after `start`.

- **No tokens are returned, and `POST /auth/session {"action":"refresh"}` is gone.** A client that reads
  `accessToken` from a login response, stores it, sends it as a bearer, and refreshes on a timer will find
  the field absent and the action `400 validation_failed`. Delete all of it: send `credentials: 'include'`,
  echo the CSRF header, and let the backend refresh. There is nothing to schedule and no expiry to watch.
- **Call `GET /auth/session` on load.** The browser can no longer inspect a token to know whether it is
  signed in, so the server has to be asked. Its 401 is an **answer**, not an error, and carries
  `extra.message.code` — one of `SESSION_EXPIRED`, `SESSION_REVOKED`, `SESSION_REVOKED_ALL`,
  `NOT_LOGGED_IN` — which is what lets a page say why rather than just showing a login form.
- **`POST /auth/password` is authenticated.** The public `forgot` / `reset` pair is gone. Recovery is
  email-OTP login: `POST /auth/login` with `step: otp-request` works for **any** active account, not only
  passwordless ones, and the password is then set or changed from inside the session. That raises the bar —
  the old flow needed only the mailbox, this needs the mailbox and a session.

tags.name: Settings
tags.description:
What a signed-in user changes about their own account — seven surfaces, and they do not behave alike.

**Second factors** (biometric sign-in, the authenticator app) are switches here rather than factors to enrol: turning one off accepts any one of four alternative proofs, retires every credential of that kind, and signs out every other session.

**The Payment PIN** has a different shape — status, verify, act — and is not a sign-in factor: it authorises payments, so changing or removing it signs nobody out.

**The email address** moves the account's primary identifier, so changing it reserves the address it leaves, revokes every session, and mails the released address a single-use link that can undo the change without a session.

**The password** is three operations on one route, split by what the caller can prove rather than by what the account has; all three revoke every other session.

**The username** is a profile setting rather than a security one, and is the only surface here with a paid-change allowance counted in Postgres rather than in Redis.

**The anti-phishing code** is the odd one out: it is not a credential at all. It is a short string this service prints in the mail it sends, so a reader can tell a genuine message from a forgery — nothing accepts it as proof of identity, it cannot stand in for an emailed code or a factor, and changing it signs nobody out. What guards it is the emailed code plus a 24-hour freeze after any email change, because the message carrying the account-recovery link carries this code too.

**Social accounts** attach a third-party provider to the account so it can be used to sign in later. It is the only surface here that leaves the service mid-flow, so it is also the only one that spends its proof up front: an emailed code plus one enrolled factor buys a sixty-second ticket, the ticket buys the trip to the provider, and the server-side state carries the proof back. The callback never mints a session - a provider identity that already belongs to somebody else is refused, not signed in to.

Every surface here requires an emailed code from `POST /auth/2fa {"action":"credential-otp"}`. None of them mints its own.

post.description:
Eight steps on one route, discriminated on `step`.

`start` creates the registration and returns an opaque `signupId`; every later step sends it back in the request body. There is no registration id in any body and no cookie involved: the temporary `orebit_reg` cookie and its `X-Registration-Token` alternative have both been removed, so a native client and a browser drive this route identically.

The server remains authoritative for the flow. `step` says which operation to run; the registration row says which are legal right now, and a step attempted from the wrong state is refused with `registration_step_invalid` (409) carrying the real state. Order: `start` → `verify-email` → `credentials` → `country`, with `resend-otp`, `check-referral`, `trust-device` and `state` available where the state machine allows.

`country` is the step that creates the account. It issues `orebit_session` and `orebit_csrf`, and it retires the `signupId` in the same transaction — replaying one afterwards answers `registration_not_found`.

201.description: Step accepted. The payload shape depends on the step: `start` returns RegistrationStart, `check-referral` returns ReferralCheck, and every other step returns RegistrationState — with a `session` block on `country`.

Set-Cookie.description:
No registration cookie is issued on any step — the flow is named by the `signupId` in the response body and the request bodies that follow it.

The `country` step issues `orebit_session` and `orebit_csrf`, because it is the step that creates the account and mints the first session — see the `Session` schema.

`orebit_device` may also be set here, on any step, if the request arrived without it — see the API description.

Public. Which captcha providers this deployment currently offers, and the public site key for each, so the login and registration pages do not carry their own copy of the server’s configuration.

`providers` is a LIST because several may be live at once. Render the first, or offer a choice, and echo the one you used back as `captchaProvider` on the request that spends the token — `POST /auth/register {"step":"start"}`, `POST /auth/login {"mode":"password"}` or `POST /auth/login {"mode":"otp-request"}`.

Re-read this before building such a request rather than caching it indefinitely. The list can change WITHOUT a deploy: an operator may take a provider out of rotation at any time. A page holding a stale list and naming a withdrawn provider gets `503 captcha_provider_unavailable` — re-read and retry with another provider. That refusal does NOT count toward the captcha failure penalty, so it costs the caller nothing but the round trip.

`enabled` is a rendering hint only. It is false exactly when `providers` is empty, which happens in a local environment with no provider configured; it never means the server will skip verification.

post.description:
Seven steps on one route, discriminated on `step`.

**The first real login operation creates the flow.** There is no separate "start" request: `password`, `otp-request` and `oauth-start` each open a `LoginAttempt` server-side as part of doing their actual work and return the opaque `loginId` naming it. None of them accepts a `loginId` — there is no flow to continue yet, and sending one is a 400.

This replaced an earlier `step: start` whose only product was a handle for the next request. A client that still sends it now gets `validation_failed`.

Every CONTINUATION step requires `loginId`: `otp-verify`, `oauth-callback`, `oauth-register` and `state`. `otp-request` is the one step that is both — with a handle it is a resend on the existing flow, without one it opens a new one.

The same handle continues to `POST /auth/2fa/verify`; no second token is issued when a second factor is required. Note that `otp-verify` takes NO identifier: the address is read from the flow the code was sent for, so a code and a recipient cannot be paired by the caller.

The flow is bound to the device and network that opened it, expires absolutely, and is single-use — a `loginId` stops resolving the instant a session is issued. A step attempted from the wrong state answers `mfa_step_invalid` (409) carrying the real state; an unknown, spent or superseded handle answers `mfa_token_invalid` (401), and one that ran out of time answers `mfa_expired` (410).

There is no temporary login cookie. Only the terminal `session` outcome sets cookies, and it sets `orebit_session` and `orebit_csrf`.

No other cookie is issued by this route. In particular there is no temporary login cookie, and `oauth-register` no longer sets one: it returns a `signupId` in the body instead. `orebit_device` may be set on any step if the request arrived without it — see the API description.

post.summary: Log out or revoke (3 actions on `action`)
post.description:
**`refresh` is gone.** The backend holds both tokens in a server-side record and rotates them itself, on whichever ordinary request finds the access token near expiry, so there is nothing left for a client to ask for. `{"action":"refresh"}` is now `400 validation_failed`.

Public **and** wrapped in an optional auth guard, deliberately — and it is the logout actions that need it. A repeated logout has to keep succeeding, and a user whose session expired while they were away must still end up signed out, so a mandatory guard would answer 401 to exactly the requests whose purpose is to clean up after a session that is already over. The optional guard still **throws on a credential that is present and malformed**.

**The credential is the `orebit_session` cookie**, an opaque handle naming the server-side record. Browser clients must send this request with credentials included (`fetch(…, { credentials: 'include' })`).

**Every unsafe method in this service requires a CSRF token when it authenticates by cookie**, and it is checked in the guard rather than here. Read the `orebit_csrf` cookie — the one cookie in this service deliberately not HttpOnly — and echo its value verbatim in the `X-Orebit-Csrf` header. The token is bound to the session handle and survives every rotation, so it does not need re-reading between calls. A client on another origin cannot read the cookie at all and should take the value from `GET /auth/session` or `GET /auth/me`.

**The two logout actions differ in blast radius.** `logout` ends every live session on the *calling device* — that is what makes closing one tab sign the user out of the other tabs in the same browser, and it is the action a normal sign-out button should send. `logout-all` ends every live session on *every* device, and should be offered only where the user has explicitly asked to be signed out everywhere.

`revoke-session` ends one *named* session — the "that is not me" button on the session list. It needs a live session of its own, and it leaves the caller's own cookies untouched.

Device grouping keys on the `orebit_device` cookie recorded when each session was minted, so `logout` still scopes correctly even if the cookie has since been cleared. Sessions issued before device cookies existed carry a coarser legacy value that could collide across devices; those are never grouped, and `logout` falls back to ending that one family alone.

parameters.name: X-Orebit-Csrf
parameters.description: The `orebit_csrf` cookie value, echoed verbatim. Required on any request carrying the `orebit_session` cookie; omitting it is `403 csrf_invalid`.

revokeSession.summary: End one named session from the session list

201.description: `logout` and `logout-all` return `{ message: { code: "LOGGED_OUT", … } }`. `revoke-session` returns `{ ok: true }`.

Set-Cookie.description:
On `logout` and `logout-all`: `orebit_session` and `orebit_csrf` are both expired, after the session has been revoked in PostgreSQL and its record dropped from Redis — in that order, so a failure can never leave a live session whose handle nobody holds.

On `revoke-session`: nothing. That action ends a *different* browser's session; the caller's own credential is untouched and must keep working.

400.description:
Validation failure — including `{"action":"refresh"}`, which no longer exists, and any body carrying a `refreshToken` field, which the schemas now reject rather than silently strip.

Error `type` values seen on this operation: `validation_failed`

401.description:
`revoke-session` was called without a live session. The two logout actions do not answer 401 for a dead session — that is the whole reason this route sits behind the optional guard.

Error `type` values seen on this operation: `unauthenticated`, `token_invalid`

403.description:
The request carried the `orebit_session` cookie but no usable CSRF token: the `X-Orebit-Csrf` header was absent, did not match the `orebit_csrf` cookie, or was issued for a different session handle. Re-read the cookie, or take the value from `GET /auth/session`.

Error `type` values seen on this operation: `csrf_invalid`

500.description:
Unexpected failure.

Error `type` values seen on this operation: `internal_error`

503.description:
Redis could not be reached, so the record naming this session could not be read — meaning the revocation could not even be attempted. **The cookies are deliberately NOT cleared**: the handle is the only value naming this session, and dropping it would strand a live session nobody could ever revoke. Retry.

get.summary: Am I signed in, and if not, why?
get.description:
The route a page calls on load. It exists because the browser now holds an opaque handle and nothing else: it cannot inspect a token's expiry, cannot count down to one, and cannot tell "I was never signed in" from "I was signed in and something ended it". The server is the only party that knows.

**Both answers carry the same three fields**, so a client reads one shape whether it arrived as a 200 or a 401 — on the 401 they are in `extra` on the problem document, with `authenticated: false`. `message.code` is the discriminant worth switching on:

- `LOGGED_IN` — the 200.
- `SESSION_EXPIRED` — the idle window closed, or the session record is gone. Nobody ended it.
- `SESSION_REVOKED` — one sign-in was ended, from another device or by a replay.
- `SESSION_REVOKED_ALL` — every sign-in was ended: a logout-all, a password change, a disabled factor, an email change.
- `NOT_LOGGED_IN` — no session cookie was presented at all.

`message.text` is a default you may show or replace; `message.code` is the contract.

**It answers only that question.** The profile and the CSRF token are not in the response: ask `GET /auth/me` for who you are and for the `x-orebit-csrf` value to echo. A liveness probe you are invited to poll has no business shipping a full profile per call, and two routes returning the same account is two answers that can disagree.

The CSRF **cookie** is still repaired here. A request arriving without a usable `orebit_csrf` — a client whose double-submit pair is already broken — gets a fresh one issued, which is the `Set-Cookie` documented on the 200. A usable one is left untouched, so a background poll cannot break an in-flight save.

**Polling this does not keep a session alive.** It is marked as not counting toward activity, deliberately: a client talking to itself must not be able to hold an abandoned tab's session open forever.

Cache-Control.description: Always `no-store`, on the 200 and on the 401. An intermediary caching "you are logged in" would serve it to the next caller on that connection.

Set-Cookie.description: Nothing on the common path. `orebit_csrf` is re-issued only when the request arrived without a usable one — a client whose double-submit pair is already broken, and whose mutations are already failing.

401.description:
Not signed in — and this is an **answer**, not an error. `extra` carries the same three fields the 200 does, including `message.code` and the `lastActiveAt` of the session that ended. Both cookies are expired on this path, so the browser stops presenting a dead handle and the next sign-in is not refused for carrying a CSRF token bound to the old one.

Error `type` values seen on this operation: `unauthenticated`, `session_expired`, `session_revoked`, `session_reuse_detected`, `token_expired`, `token_invalid`

Set-Cookie.description: `orebit_session` and `orebit_csrf` are both expired. Not on a 503 — see that response.

Unexpected failure.

Error `type` values seen on this operation: `internal_error`

503.description:
Redis could not be reached while resolving the session record. Not a statement about whether anyone is signed in, so it carries no `message` and **does not clear the cookies**. Retry.

post.summary: Set or change a password (3 actions on `action`)
post.description:
**Authenticated** — this route is no longer recovery, and a client still calling the old public `forgot` / `reset` gets a 401.

The split is by what you can *prove*, not by what you have:

- `change` — you know the current password. No email round trip. Deliberately does NOT accept an emailed code: two proofs for one action means the weaker one is the only one that matters.
- `set` — you can read the account's email. Serves both the account that never had a password and the user who has forgotten theirs.
- `request-code` — sends the code `set` consumes.

Both writing actions revoke every **other** session and email the account. The caller's own session survives.

post.summary: Trust or forget this device (2 actions on `action`)
post.description:
Authenticated. `trust` remembers **the browser that sent the request** — identified by its `orebit_device` cookie, never by a body field, so a caller cannot trust a device they are not holding. `untrust` forgets one by id and revokes every session that trust was holding open.

Running after authentication rather than during it is why password, email-OTP and Google login all get remember-me without threading a `rememberMe` flag through three flows.

get.description:
Authenticated. One entry per browser, with the sessions on it and whether it is trusted. Grouped rather than flat because a device is what a user recognises — "my phone" is one row with three tabs under it, not three unexplained sessions — and because trust is only revocable at that level.

`current: true` marks the device and the session making this request, so a client can warn before revoking the one the user is sitting on.

get.summary: What is enrolled on this account
get.description:
Authenticated. Lists confirmed factors and how many recovery codes remain.

Authenticated. One route, ten actions, discriminated on `action`.

─── The two-step shape ───

─── update and disable ───

**This route is public.** Two of its three actions require a session and refuse without one; the third — `recover-start` — is authorised by a token mailed to a released address and deliberately does not read a session at all.

─── start ───

Authenticated. Validates the address, fixes the security tier, and mails a code to every mailbox that must answer: the address held now, the address being claimed, and any previously released address still inside its retention window. Returns `requiredTargets`, which is what a client renders its input boxes from.

The tier and the address are recorded server-side and read from there at completion. A change started against a passkey cannot be finished with a password, and a challenge minted for one address cannot be completed against another.

Starting again supersedes any change already in flight — there is one per account.

`skipRetainedEmail` is for the user whose previous mailbox is unreachable. It waives that code and expires the retention, and is refused unless the declared tier is an authenticator, a passkey or KYC — on an account whose only proof is a password, an attacker holding that password could otherwise shed the record the real owner needs.

─── resend ───

Authenticated. Re-sends ONE code. Per-target deliberately: issuing a code supersedes the live one for its purpose, so a resend-everything would invalidate the codes the user has already found.

─── recover-start ───

NOT authenticated. `recoveryId` is the token from the "your email was changed — did you do this?" message. `intent: "restore"` puts the account back on the released address; `intent: "replace"` moves it to a third address named here, and mails a code to both. Send the token in the BODY, never in a query string.

Recovery does not consume the change budget: charging it would let whoever performed the change exhaust the budget and thereby block the recovery.

**This route is public**, for the same reason as the one above: a completed change revokes every session and the released address cannot sign in, so the person a recovery exists for is precisely the one who cannot authenticate. A body carrying `challengeId` is a change and requires a session; one carrying `recoveryId` is a recovery and does not.

─── Completing a change ───

Carries every code the ceremony demanded plus the security proof for the tier it was started with. All of it in one request, and the address moves in one transaction — there is no separate completion step, because the challenge already holds the address and the tier.

The codes are spent BEFORE the security proof, so a wrong code cannot be used to probe whether a password guess was right. A code sent to one address will not satisfy the proof for another: each is bound to its recipient.

`method` must match the tier the change was started with. A request naming a different one is refused rather than run, which is what makes the downgrade impossible rather than merely checked. Conflicting proofs — a password beside a passkey — are refused at validation, before any comparison.

On success: the address moves, the released one is reserved for the retention period, EVERY session is revoked, and the released address is mailed a recovery link.

─── Completing a recovery ───

Carries the code sent to the released address, plus — for `replace` — the code sent to the third address. No security factor: the token proves the mailbox, and every operation it authorises points the account at an address proved in the same request. Every session is revoked. A `restore` drops the retention because the address is the account's again; a `replace` keeps it with a fresh window and a fresh token.

─── A previous availability check is never trusted ───

Whoever saves second is refused with `username_unavailable`, and that is ordinary behaviour rather than an error condition: the only authority is this write, taken under a lock against a unique index. post.summary: Set, reset, or recover the account password
post.description:
Authenticated. One route, three operations on an `action` discriminant. The split is by WHAT THE CALLER CAN PROVE, not by what the account has — a user who has forgotten their password HAS one, so an operation gated on "no password exists" does not apply to them and one gated on "prove the current password" demands the very thing they cannot supply.

─── set ───

For an account with NO password: one created through a provider, or one that skipped the step at signup. Authorised by the emailed code alone, and bounded by what it can do — it CREATES a credential, so there is nothing to overwrite. Refused with `password_already_set` when a password exists, including when a concurrent request creates one first: the unique index is the arbiter, so two simultaneous calls produce one password and one conflict, never a silent overwrite.

─── reset ───

For an account whose owner knows the current password. Requires the emailed code AND `currentPassword` — both, never either, because accepting one as an alternative to the other would make the weaker of them the only one that matters. A wrong `currentPassword` answers `invalid_credentials` and counts toward the durable lockout ladder like any other password guess.

─── forgot ───

For an account whose owner cannot supply the current password. Requires the emailed code, AND one additional factor if the account has one:

  no factor           the emailed code is sufficient. A `passkey` or `totpCode` sent anyway is refused with `mfa_method_unavailable` rather than ignored.
  passkey only        a WebAuthn assertion in `passkey`.
  authenticator only  a code in `totpCode`.
  both enrolled       either one. Send exactly ONE — a body carrying both is `validation_failed`, so the weaker cannot silently become the only one checked.

THE BACKEND DECIDES whether a factor is required, from the account's confirmed credentials. There is no request field that asserts it, and sending one is a validation error. When a factor is required and none is presented, the answer is `password_factor_required` with `extra.methods` naming what would be accepted — read `GET /settings/security/password` first to render the right prompt.

─── The emailed code, and the WebAuthn challenge ───

Neither is minted here. Request the code with `POST /auth/2fa {"action":"credential-otp"}` and the assertion options with `POST /auth/2fa {"action":"reauth-challenge"}`. A password-shaped copy of either would be a second way to mint the same credential, metered by a second bucket.

The code is consumed BEFORE the additional factor is verified, so a caller cannot use a wrong code to probe whether a TOTP guess was right. The consequence is that a wrong factor spends a good code.

─── Effects, on all three ───

Every path ends the account's other sessions and emails the owner. The calling session is kept.

All three are frozen for 24 hours after an email change (`security_cooldown`), `forgot` included — it is the path that needs no knowledge of the current password, so it is the one an attacker who has just moved the address would take.

post.summary: Set, change, or replace the anti-phishing code
post.description:
Authenticated. One route, three operations on an `action` discriminant.

The anti-phishing code is a short string the account owner chooses, which we print in the emails we send them so they can tell a genuine message from a forgery. IT IS NOT A CREDENTIAL: nothing accepts it as proof of identity, it cannot substitute for an emailed code, a password, a passkey or 2FA, and changing it signs nobody out. An attacker who learns it gains no access to the account — what they gain is the ability to write convincing mail, which is why it is encrypted at rest and never returned by the API.

─── set ───

For an account with NO code. Authorised by the emailed code alone, and bounded by what it can do — it CREATES a value where there was none, so there is nothing to overwrite. Refused with `anti_phishing_code_already_set` when one exists, including when a concurrent request sets one first: the write is predicated on the column being empty, so two simultaneous calls produce one code and one conflict, never a silent overwrite.

─── change ───

For an owner who knows their current code. Requires the emailed code AND `currentCode`.

`currentCode` IS NOT A SECURITY BOUNDARY, and should not be presented to users as one: `replace` below reaches the identical write without it, so anyone able to call `change` can call `replace` instead. It exists so a user who misremembers their code is TOLD, rather than overwriting a value they will then fail to recognise in their own mail. A wrong one answers `anti_phishing_code_incorrect` as a 400, and — deliberately — does not consume the emailed code, so a typo costs a round trip rather than a fresh email.

─── replace ───

For an owner who cannot produce their current code. Requires the emailed code alone, and demands NO passkey, authenticator or password.

That is deliberate and is not a weakening: the value lives in the user’s inbox rather than in their memory, so someone who has not read an Orebit email in months genuinely cannot supply it, and gating the change on a value only old mail contains would strand them with a code they can neither recognise nor replace. Demanding a factor would buy no security — the code guards nothing — and would lock every account without one out of a setting it is entitled to change.

─── The emailed code ───

Every operation requires one, in `emailCode`. Request it with `POST /auth/2fa {"action":"credential-otp"}` — there is no anti-phishing-specific endpoint for it, because a second way to mint the same credential would be metered by a second bucket.

─── The format ───

6 to 30 characters, letters and digits only, case preserved and compared exactly. Spaces, punctuation and non-ASCII are refused, and a value with leading or trailing whitespace is REFUSED rather than trimmed. The narrow alphabet is the point: this value is compared by eye against an email, so anything that renders ambiguously — a Cyrillic homoglyph, a zero-width character, collapsible whitespace — would let two different stored codes look identical and defeat the comparison the feature rests on.

─── What is frozen, and when ───

All three operations are refused for 24 hours after the account’s email address changes (`security_cooldown`). The reason is specific: the "your email address was changed — did you do this?" message goes to the address the account just left, carries the recovery link, AND carries this code. Without the freeze an attacker who had just moved the address could also change the code, so the genuine owner would see an unfamiliar one on the single message that gives them their account back.

The code is never echoed in a response, and never appears in an error body.

--- What is required ---

- authenticator only -> `emailCode` + `totpCode`

- both enrolled -> `emailCode` + EITHER, the caller's choice

A recovery code is never accepted here, and neither is the account password. A printed backup sheet may take a lost factor off an account and must never attach a credential to one.

The delay is the point. Removing a social login is reachable by anyone holding a live session and the mailbox, so the change is announced and then waited out - whoever did not ask for it has a week to notice.

--- Nothing about your session changes ---

No `Set-Cookie`, no session rotation, no token issuance, no sign-out. `GET /auth/me` returns the same user before and after.

post.description:
Authenticated AND behind a single-use elevation ticket proved for `account.delete`. Obtain one from `POST /settings/security/delete-account/verify {"action":"verify"}`.

--- THIS TAKES EFFECT IMMEDIATELY ---

Unlike the delayed social unlink, nothing here is a notice period. On success the account's status moves to DELETED and EVERY session is revoked, including the one that made this call. The token that authorised this request is dead by the time the response is read, and no login path of any kind will mint another.

What waits is the DATA. Until `purgeAt` the account is LOCKED, not gone, and stays fully restorable through `POST /settings/security/delete-account/reactivate`.

At `purgeAt`, thirty days out, it is PERMANENTLY DELETED: the user record and every child record are physically removed from the database, the remaining PII is scrubbed, recovery becomes impossible rather than merely refused, and the email and username are released for re-registration. There is no undo after that point.

--- Idempotent ---

Asking again inside the window returns the ORIGINAL `purgeAt` and writes nothing. The countdown is never extended by a second request.

--- Withdrawals are out of scope ---

`acknowledgeFundsForfeited` records a user's answer to a prompt. It withdraws nothing and forfeits nothing: there is no wallet, ledger or Withdraw Funds API in this service. It is read only when a bound withdrawal provider reports pending funds, which nothing does today.

post.summary: Prove yourself and earn a ticket to delete the account
post.description:
Authenticated. Two actions on one route: `challenge` reports what this account can prove, `verify` spends the proof and returns a single-use elevation ticket.

An emailed code is required on EVERY path, for every account, whether or not a factor is enrolled - request it with `POST /auth/2fa {"action":"credential-otp"}`. On top of that, send exactly one enrolled factor: `totpCode` or `passkey`. An account with neither enrolled owes nothing further, and naming a factor it does not hold is refused.

The account PASSWORD is never accepted here, deliberately: it is the credential most likely to be already compromised in the case this ceremony exists to stop.

The ticket is bound to this session and to `account.delete` alone. It cannot be spent on a factor change, a social link, or `POST /auth/link`, and no ticket earned for those can be spent on a deletion.

post.description:
PUBLIC - no session required, and that is deliberate rather than an oversight. Deleting an account revokes every session it had and its status refuses every sign-in path, so the person who needs this route is always, by construction, someone who cannot authenticate. What stands in for the session is a code mailed to the account's own address.

Two actions: `challenge` mails a code, `verify` spends it and restores the account.

--- This endpoint does not reveal whether an account exists ---

The `challenge` action returns the SAME body and the SAME status for a live account, a deleted one, a purged one, and an address that never registered. It also charges the same rate-limit buckets in all four cases, so throttling cannot be used as an oracle either. A live account is deliberately sent no mail at all.

The `verify` action answers `otp_invalid` for a wrong code AND for an unknown address, so the two remain indistinguishable.

--- The window is enforced by the server ---

Restoration succeeds only while `now < purgeAt`. Past it the user record has been physically deleted, so there is nothing to restore — the account cannot be recovered by any means, and cannot be distinguished from an address that never registered.

--- Restoring does not sign you in ---

No cookie is set and no token is issued. The sessions the deletion revoked do not come back; the owner signs in again through the ordinary login.

BearerAuth.description:
**Browsers do not use this.** A browser authenticates with the `orebit_session` cookie, and no access token is returned in any response body — see the `Session` schema.

This scheme is kept for callers that are not browsers: a script, an integration test, a service. The token is the same ES256, 15-minute access token the cookie resolves to, verified the same way — the guard checks the signature and audience *and* that the session has not been revoked. Obtaining one requires signing in through a non-browser path that can read it, so in practice this is for tooling that mints its own.

A bearer caller needs no CSRF token: nothing is attached ambiently, so there is no cross-site request to forge.

SessionCookie.name: orebit_session
SessionCookie.description: The browser session cookie set by `POST /auth/login`. Chat uses this and nothing else: no token in the address, a header or the socket `auth` payload. In a browser, send requests with `credentials: "include"`; in Swagger UI sign in first and the cookie is sent for you.

CsrfHeader.name: x-orebit-csrf
CsrfHeader.description: Every POST/PUT needs the CSRF header: copy the value of the `orebit_csrf` cookie (the same value `POST /auth/login` returns as `session.csrfToken`). GET routes do not need it.

Problem.description: RFC 9457 problem detail. Every non-2xx response uses this shape with content type `application/problem+json`. `type` is a stable machine-readable slug from src/contracts.ts — branch on it, not on the human-readable `title`.

extra.description: Operation-specific context, e.g. `attemptsRemaining` on `otp_invalid`, `state` on `registration_step_invalid`, `email` on `oauth_link_required`.

PublicUser.description: The API-boundary projection of a user. Exactly these eight fields.

publicCode.description: Shareable account identifier: the prefix `OREBiT` plus 8 characters.

username.description: Generated at signup from the email local-part; not user-chosen.

country.description: ISO 3166-1 alpha-2. Trimmed and uppercased server-side, then validated against the 249-code list in src/utils/country.ts.

referralCode.description: This user's own code, for referring others.

hasPassword.description: False for accounts created via a provider or with the password step skipped. Such accounts can also sign in by email OTP.

Session.description:
A freshly issued session, and **no tokens at all** — that absence is the contract, and it can be asserted structurally: no field here is a credential.

Both tokens live in a server-side record. The browser receives `Set-Cookie` for `orebit_session`, an opaque handle naming that record (HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, `Path=/`), and `orebit_csrf`, which script *can* read. Send no `Authorization` header; send the request with credentials included and echo the CSRF value in `X-Orebit-Csrf` on every unsafe method.

The access token used to be here, because it had to go into a header — which meant it had to be readable, which meant an XSS stole a working credential and, with the refresh cookie the browser attached automatically, the ability to mint more. Both token expiries went with the tokens: they described a refresh cycle the client no longer takes part in.

csrfToken.description: Echo verbatim in `X-Orebit-Csrf` on every unsafe method. Also in the readable `orebit_csrf` cookie — reported here for clients on another origin, which cannot read it. Bound to the session handle, so it survives every rotation and does not need re-reading between calls.

expiresAt.description: When this session dies if nothing else happens. A *sliding* deadline, not a promise: activity pushes it out, and a revocation ignores it entirely.

SessionStatus.description:
The answer from `GET /auth/session` when the caller IS signed in.

The same three field names the 401 carries in `extra`, so a client reads one shape either way. `authenticated` is the discriminant and is a literal on both sides.

The profile and the CSRF token are NOT here — this route answers whether you are signed in, and `GET /auth/me` answers who you are and which token to echo.

lastActiveAt.description: When this session was last active, as the row records it — not `now`. Null only when the answer came from the cached-revocation fast path, which deliberately never queries.

SessionMessage.description: Why the session is in the state it is in. `code` is the contract; `text` is a default you may show or replace — a client that branched on wording would break the day the wording was improved.

text.example: You have been logged out due to inactivity.

Logout.description: The answer from `POST /auth/session`. Says what happened, as opposed to what the state is — which is why `LOGGED_OUT` is not one of `SessionMessage`'s five codes: the guard can never *observe* it, and the session it describes is already revoked by the time it is serialised.

signupId.description: Opaque handle for this registration, returned by `step: start` and required on every later step. 32 bytes of CSPRNG output, base64url. NOT the registration's database id — only a peppered hash is stored server-side, and the row id never leaves the server. Hold it in memory for the life of the signup; do not persist it. Retired the moment `country` completes the row.

session.description: Present only on the terminal `country` step, which creates the account.

A provider whose credentials are absent on this deployment is refused with `oauth_provider_unsupported` (400, naming the provider) rather than a validation error, so the wire contract does not change when a deployment gains credentials.

X and TELEGRAM cannot create accounts, permanently: X exposes no email address through OAuth 2.0 at any access tier, and a Telegram account is a phone number. They sign in an account that has already linked them, and can be attached to an existing one.

TELEGRAM has no authorization endpoint — `oauth-start` returns a null `url` and `flow: signed-payload`.

Note this step WRITES an unconfirmed factor, unlike the passkey equivalent whose challenge is ephemeral. amountMinor.description: Minor units (cents) as an integer. Null when the next change is free.

UsernameReservationEntry.description: A previous username still held for this account.

expiresAt.description: After this, anyone may take it.

reclaimFree.description: Whether taking it back is free even with the allowance spent. True for the long, identity-protecting reservation left by the first change in a sequence; false for the few-minute release left by subsequent ones.

UsernameStatus.description: The username screen, in one payload. Every value is decided by the backend — the applicable minimum length, the remaining free changes, whether the next one is paid.

username.description: As displayed, in the casing it was claimed with.

active.description: Determined by the backend from the entitlement system. Never accepted from a client.

reservations.description: Newest deadline first. Empty for an account that has never changed its username.

UsernameIssue.description: One thing wrong with a proposed username. `code` is stable and switchable; `message` is complete copy for a client that does not switch.

UsernameAvailability.description: Whether a username can be used. Note that an INVALID username is reported here with `available: false` and `reason: "invalid"` rather than as a 400 — this operation is called on a keystroke debounce, where a half-typed name is expected input rather than a malformed request.

username.description: The NORMALISED form of what was asked about. Echoed so a client can discard a response that arrived after the user typed on.

reason.description: Absent when available. `reserved` means a previous owner still holds it and never says who. `current` means the caller already has it.

issues.description: Present only for `reason: "invalid"`. Every problem at once, so a form marks them all in one pass.

suggestions.description: Present only when unavailable. Each one has been checked against the authoritative state before being offered — though, like any availability answer, it can still be taken before the user saves.

UsernameUpdateRequest.description: The entire contract. Additional properties are REFUSED, not ignored — a client cannot submit `isPremium` or a price.

reservedUntil.description: Nobody else may take it before this. Long for the first change in a sequence, a few minutes for subsequent ones.

PasswordOperationStatus.description: Whether one password operation is open on this account.

reason.description: Present only when `available` is false. A short, user-facing sentence.

PasswordStatus.description:
The password screen, in one payload.

The client asks this one question and renders everything from the answer. It never has to work out whether a password exists, whether a factor is enrolled, or which of the three operations applies — those are policy, they are decided by the backend, and a client that re-derived them would be a second copy of the rules that nobody updates.

passwordSet.description: Whether a password credential exists. False for an account created through a provider and for one that skipped the password at signup.

factorRequired.description: Whether `action: "forgot"` will additionally demand a passkey assertion or a TOTP code. True exactly when this account has a CONFIRMED passkey or authenticator. The backend decides this; a client cannot assert it.

methods.description: Which factors would be accepted, in offer order (`passkey` first). Empty when `factorRequired` is false.

PasswordChanged.description: The password changed. Carries no password and no hash — the value the caller sent is the only copy that ever existed outside argon2.

operation.description: Echoed from the server's own dispatch, not from the request.

factorVerified.description: Which additional factor was actually proved. Always null on `set` and `reset`, which cannot verify one, and null on `forgot` for an account that has no factor.

otherSessionsRevoked.description: Always true. Every one of the three operations ends the account's OTHER sessions; the calling session is kept. That is what makes a password change a usable response to a compromise.

AntiPhishingStatus.description:
The anti-phishing screen, in one payload.

One boolean, because the three operations partition it exactly — a per-operation table would be three fields derivable from this one, which is three chances for a client to render a contradiction.

Deliberately carries neither the code nor the date it was set.

configured.description: Whether an anti-phishing code is set. When false, offer `set`; when true, offer `change` and `replace`. Decided by the backend from the stored row — a client cannot assert it.

oneOf.title: set
oneOf.description: Create the first code. Refused when one is already set.

code.description: The new code. 6–30 characters, letters and digits only. Case is preserved and significant. Leading or trailing whitespace is refused rather than trimmed.

emailCode.description: The emailed code, from `POST /auth/2fa {"action":"credential-otp"}`. Required on every action.

oneOf.title: change
oneOf.description: Replace a code the caller knows. `currentCode` is mistake-prevention, not authorisation — see the operation description.

currentCode.description: The code currently set. Bounded but deliberately not format-checked, so a stored value is never rejected on composition.

code.description: The new code. 6–30 characters, letters and digits only. Case is preserved and significant. Leading or trailing whitespace is refused rather than trimmed.

emailCode.description: The emailed code, from `POST /auth/2fa {"action":"credential-otp"}`. Required on every action.

oneOf.title: replace
oneOf.description: Replace a code the caller cannot produce. The emailed code is the whole authorisation; no factor is required.

code.description: The new code. 6–30 characters, letters and digits only. Case is preserved and significant. Leading or trailing whitespace is refused rather than trimmed.

emailCode.description: The emailed code, from `POST /auth/2fa {"action":"credential-otp"}`. Required on every action.

AntiPhishingUpdated.description:
The code was written.

Carries no code — the user sees it in their next email, which is the channel this feature is about.

action.description: Which operation ran, echoed from the server’s own dispatch rather than from the request, so an integration bug shows up as a mismatch rather than as a confident wrong label.

otherSessionsRevoked.description: Always false, and stated rather than left to be assumed. No session was ever established with an anti-phishing code, so there is nothing for a sweep to invalidate.

RegisterTrustDevice.description: "Trust this device and stay signed in?", asked on the screen before `country`. Optional: a client that never sends it completes with `trustDevice` false and gets an ordinary session. Legal only from `CREDENTIALS_SET`, and it does not advance the state, so it may be re-sent as the user changes their mind.

signupId.description: Opaque handle for this registration, returned by `step: start` and required on every later step. 32 bytes of CSPRNG output, base64url. NOT the registration's database id — only a peppered hash is stored server-side, and the row id never leaves the server. Hold it in memory for the life of the signup; do not persist it. Retired the moment `country` completes the row.

LoginState.description: Read the flow's own progress back, for a client that holds a live `loginId` but has lost track of which step it is on — a reloaded page, or the return leg of an OAuth round trip. Answers the same outcome the step that produced the current state would have.

loginId.description: Opaque handle for this sign-in, returned by `step: start` and required on every later step of this route AND on `POST /auth/2fa/verify`. 32 bytes of CSPRNG output, base64url. One handle for the whole flow — no second token is issued when a second factor is required. Hold it in memory; do not persist it. Retired the moment a session is issued.

LoginStartedOutcome.description: A flow exists and nothing has been proven on it yet. Reached only by `step: state` reading back a sign-in parked mid-OAuth — no request creates a flow and stops there, because the step that opens one always goes on to do its actual work.

loginId.description: Opaque handle for this sign-in, returned by `step: start` and required on every later step of this route AND on `POST /auth/2fa/verify`. 32 bytes of CSPRNG output, base64url. One handle for the whole flow — no second token is issued when a second factor is required. Hold it in memory; do not persist it. Retired the moment a session is issued.

SocialAccountLink.description:
One linked provider, as the settings screen shows it.

Carries no provider subject - see the note on `GET /settings/security/social-accounts`. Every display field is nullable because the five providers genuinely differ in what they publish; fall back from `displayName` to `email` to the provider name.

A pending removal is carried by `unlinkAt` - see that field. The row is still a live link until then.

displayName.description: The name the provider asserted when the link was made. Null for Apple, which publishes none in its ID token and offers no endpoint to fetch one, and null for links made before this was recorded.

email.description: The address the provider asserted at link time, kept as provenance. `GET /auth/me` stays authoritative for the account's own address. Null for X and Telegram, which supply none.

emailVerifiedByProvider.description: Whether the provider asserted it had verified that address.

lastLoginAt.description: When this provider was last used to sign in. Null until it is.

unlinkAt.description:
When this link is scheduled to be removed, or null when no removal is pending.

The account is STILL LINKED while this is set. It keeps appearing here, it keeps signing the user in, and the provider stays out of `availableProviders` because the slot is still occupied. Only after this instant does the link stop resolving.

There is no companion `unlinkPending` boolean on purpose: two fields encoding one fact are two fields that can disagree.

A client that wants to offer the way back drives it from THIS field, not from `availableProviders`: re-linking the SAME provider account cancels the removal. Linking a DIFFERENT account of that provider is refused until the deadline passes.

SocialAccountsStatus.description: The Settings -> Social accounts screen, in one payload.

availableProviders.description: Providers this deployment is configured for AND this account has not linked. Both filters are applied server-side; a client cannot derive the first from the enum, because the enum is the set of providers that EXIST while configuration decides which are OFFERED.

oneOf.title: challenge
oneOf.description: Ask what this account can prove. Takes no provider: the proof is about the account, so changing your mind between Google and Apple costs nothing.

oneOf.title: verify
oneOf.description: Prove it, and receive the ticket. Send exactly one factor, or none when the account has none enrolled. Set `intent: "unlink"` to earn a ticket for `POST /settings/security/social-accounts/unlink` instead.

emailCode.description: Required on EVERY path, whether or not a factor is enrolled. Obtain it with `POST /auth/2fa {"action":"credential-otp"}`.

totpCode.description: A code from the authenticator app. Permitted only when one is enrolled, and not alongside `passkey`.

passkey.description: A WebAuthn assertion against the challenge returned by `action: challenge`. Permitted only when a passkey is enrolled, and not alongside `totpCode`.

intent.description:
Which write the ticket this returns may be spent on.

Linking and unlinking owe the IDENTICAL proof - an emailed code on every path, plus one enrolled factor when the account has one - so they share this route. What they do not share is the resulting permit: the ticket is stamped with `account.social.link` or `account.social.unlink` and is refused at the other route. Omit it and you get a link ticket, exactly as before this field existed.

SocialLinkChallenge.description: What this account can prove before a link ceremony.

methods.description: Empty when nothing is enrolled, which is the signal to render no factor prompt at all - the emailed code alone will do. `recovery_code` never appears: a backup code cannot attach a provider.

options.description: WebAuthn assertion options, or null when this account has no passkey.

emailCodeRequired.description: Always true, and stated rather than left to be inferred from an empty `methods` array.

SocialLinkElevated.description: A single-use permit for ONE link start. Present it in the `x-elevation-ticket` header.

action.description: The one write this ticket authorises. It cannot be spent on `POST /auth/link`, nor on adding or removing a factor.

redirectUri.description: Optional. Must equal the redirect URI this deployment is configured with for that provider - anything else is refused as an open redirect.

url.description: Null for a provider with no authorization endpoint (Telegram). Not a failure - read `flow`.

state.description: Carry this to the callback. Not a secret and authorises nothing: the entry behind it is bound to this account, login, device and network.

flow.description: `signed-payload` means render the provider's widget rather than navigating.

code.description: The authorization code, or for Telegram the signed payload verbatim.

SocialAccountLinked.description: The newly linked account, in the same shape `GET /settings/security/social-accounts` returns, so a client can insert the row without a second round trip. No session payload: this operation signs nobody in.

SocialAccountUnlinkRequest.description: The provider, and deliberately nothing else. No link id, no provider subject, no user id, no token - the row is resolved from your own session plus this value, so there is no field on which to name another account's link.

SocialAccountUnlinkScheduled.description:
The removal was SCHEDULED. Nothing has been unlinked yet.

The outcome says `scheduled` rather than `unlinked` because the account is still linked when this returns and stays that way until `unlinkAt`. A client that removed the row from its list on seeing this would show the user something untrue for a week - `GET /settings/security/social-accounts` keeps listing the provider, carrying the same `unlinkAt`.

unlinkAt.description: When the link will actually be removed: seven days from the request, computed server-side. A background sweep performs the removal, so it happens at or shortly after this instant rather than exactly on it.

PendingWithdrawalsState.description:
What a bound withdrawal subsystem says about this account's funds.

IMPORTANT: `unavailable` means NO WITHDRAWAL SUBSYSTEM IS BOUND. It is not a balance of zero and must not be rendered as one. It is the only value this service returns today - the Withdraw Funds API is a future task, and there is no wallet, ledger or balance in this service. `none` means a real provider looked and found nothing; `pending` means it found funds.

status.description: `deleted` means the account is inside its recovery window. A purged account cannot reach this endpoint at all - it has no sessions and no longer resolves.

purgeAt.description: When the account is permanently erased. Null unless `status` is `deleted`.

reactivationAvailableUntil.description: The same instant as `purgeAt`, named for what the user can still do about it.

withdrawalPromptRequired.description: Whether to show a withdrawal prompt before the delete button. True only when a real provider reported funds, so false for every account today.

methods.description: Factors this account can prove. Empty means the emailed code alone will do. `recovery_code` never appears - a backup code cannot delete an account.

emailCodeRequired.description: Always true. An emailed code is owed on every path.

emailCode.description: Required on every path. Obtain it from `POST /auth/2fa {"action":"credential-otp"}`.

DeleteAccountVerifyRequest.description: Send exactly one factor when the account has any enrolled; send neither when it has none.

options.description: WebAuthn request options, or null when the account holds no passkey.

acknowledgeFundsForfeited.description: Records that the owner was shown a withdrawal prompt and chose to continue. It does NOT withdraw, forfeit or move anything - there is no withdrawal subsystem in this service. Read only when a bound provider reports `pending`, which nothing does today.

AccountReactivationRequested.description: Returned for EVERY address - live, deleted, purged, or never registered. There is nothing in this shape to vary, deliberately.

ChatRefusalReason.description: The machine-readable reason on a refusal, in `extra.reason` of the Problem body (HTTP) and of the ack error (socket). Decide what to show from this value, never from the English `detail`. `content_blocked` also carries `extra.rule` (`media_type`, `text`, `emoji`, `banned_word`, `link`, `spam`); a `403` for a ban or mute carries `extra.expiresAt`.

ChatPageInfo.description: Every list answers `{ items, nextCursor }`. Pass `nextCursor` back as `cursor` for the next page; `null` ends the list.

ChatRequirement.description: What a locked or read-only room needs, so the app can say "get plan X" or "verify KYC level Y".

id.description: Room id. Any room route also accepts the slug.

type.description: The room kind (SO = Site Owner). Stored types the server does not know are never listed.

reason.description: Why the room is closed or read-only, for display.

casinoConditions.description: Present for casino rooms: which of the conditions the user meets.

gifProvider.description: The GIF host the picker should use.

rules.description: Empty when the admin set none.

ChatMembers.description: A promo-only viewer gets the count and an empty list.

style.description: Free-form look: gradient, border colour, badge.

url.description: Chat uploads come as a signed link (`?exp=&sig=`); GIFs are plain https URLs.

ChatMessage.description: A message as every viewer receives it, over HTTP and over the socket. A retracted message is reduced to its id, room and time.

alertType.description: Only for staff, and for alerts.

hasMore.description: With `after`, true when more newer messages remain.

effectiveDefaultRoomId.description: The room to open: the last one the server remembers if still viewable, else the admin default.

ChatPreferencesUpdate.description: Both optional. `activeSkinId: null` clears the skin; a skin the user may not use is refused with `skin_not_allowed`.

clientMessageId.description: A new UUID per message, reused when you retry: a retried send is stored and broadcast once.

note.description: Optional reason, kept in the moderation record.

details.description: Optional. An empty box counts as no details.

roomId.description: Room id or slug; omit for a chat-wide warning.
Room id or slug; omit for a chat-wide ban.

durationHours.description: From 1 to the chat setting `limits.maxBanHours`. Required unless `permanent` is true.

expiresAt.description: Set from the database clock; null for a permanent ban.

url.description: The chat media URL to send in `mediaUrl`. The file is never served publicly; messages carry signed links.

ChatModuleResult.description: The result of a Module 4–9 chat route (see the route description); a REPORT-mode staff action answers `{ requested: true, requestId, permission, createdAt }`.

kind.description: BAN, a restriction kind, AD_FAILED / AD_CANCELLED / AD_REFUNDED, or GIFT_REVERTED.

ChatRoomId.name: roomId
ChatRoomId.description: A room id (UUID) or slug. Never the display name.

ChatUserHandle.name: userId
ChatUserHandle.description: A user id, username or login code.
